function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

**Java** is a high‑level, class‑based, object‑oriented programming language that was first released by Sun Microsystems in 1995 (now owned by Oracle). It’s designed to be:

| Feature | What it means |
|---------|---------------|
| **Write once, run anywhere (WORA)** | Java programs compile to bytecode that runs on any device with a Java Virtual Machine (JVM), regardless of the underlying hardware or operating system. |
| **Object‑oriented** | Everything is an object (except primitives), encouraging modular, reusable code. |
| **Strongly typed** | Types are checked at compile time, reducing runtime errors. |
| **Garbage‑collected** | Automatic memory management frees developers from manual memory handling. |
| **Secure** | The JVM sandbox, bytecode verification, and security manager help protect against malicious code. |
| **Multithreaded** | Built‑in support for concurrent execution. |

### Typical uses

| Domain | Why Java fits |
|--------|---------------|
| **Enterprise applications** | Robust libraries (Spring, Hibernate), scalability, and strong typing. |
| **Android apps** | Android’s SDK is built on Java (or Kotlin, which interoperates with Java). |
| **Web servers & app servers** | Java EE (Jakarta EE) provides standards for web services, messaging, and persistence. |
| **Big data & distributed systems** | Hadoop, Spark, and other frameworks are written in Java. |
| **Embedded systems** | Java ME (Micro Edition) targets resource‑constrained devices. |
| **Desktop GUI** | Swing, JavaFX for cross‑platform desktop apps. |

### Quick history

| Year | Milestone |
|------|-----------|
| 1991 | James Gosling starts Java project at Sun. |
| 1995 | Java 1.0 released – “write once, run anywhere.” |
| 1998 | Java 2 (J2SE) introduces Swing, JDBC, etc. |
| 2004 | Java 5 (J2SE 5.0) adds generics, annotations, enums. |
| 2011 | Oracle acquires Sun Microsystems. |
| 2014 | Java 8 introduces lambda expressions, streams. |
| 2017 | Java 9 modular system (Project Jigsaw). |
| 2020+ | Java 17, 18, 19… (LTS releases every 3 years). |

### Common misconceptions

| Myth | Reality |
|------|---------|
| **Java = JavaScript** | Completely different languages; Java is statically typed, compiled; JavaScript is dynamically typed, interpreted. |
| **Java is slow** | Modern JVMs use just‑in‑time (JIT) compilation and advanced optimizations; performance is comparable to native code for many workloads. |
| **Java is only for servers** | It’s used everywhere—from mobile to embedded to cloud. |

### Getting started

```bash
# Compile
javac HelloWorld.java

# Run
java HelloWorld
```

```java
public class HelloWorld {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, Java!");
    }
}
```

That’s the essence of Java: a versatile, mature language that powers a huge portion of today’s software ecosystem.
